pathways.climate_pressure: Climate-related seasonal water-supply pressure and rising irrigation demand.
pathways.documented_impact: Scarcity in the irrigation-dependent Dashoguz production system.
pathways.fcv_mediator: Water-intensive crops, inefficient irrigation and competing demands concentrate pressure on limited water.
pathways.possible_consequence: The 2024 risk assessment warns of possible conflict among water users; it does not report violence or dispute incidence.
alternative_explanations: Upstream withdrawals, crop choice, infrastructure losses and allocation decisions affect scarcity independently of climate.
pathways.uncertainty: A stakeholder-informed conditional mechanism, not an identified causal effect, current dispute count or armed-conflict forecast.
resilience_factors: The assessment proposes water-saving practices and coordination; the independent evaluation identifies some water-saving uptake but limited scaling.
pathways.compact_statement: Climate-related water pressure and inefficient, competing irrigation uses can create water-user disputes in Dashoguz; violence is not established.

gaps: Water-user conflict is a conditional planning risk, not observed violence or a forecast of armed conflict. No reverse-FCV interruption of adaptation was verified.
Assessment evidence is selective and partly stakeholder-informed; no current nationwide local vulnerability ranking is available.

The policy brief derives from the same risk assessment, not an independent study. Evaluation contributions do not establish counterfactual impacts; training and project objectives are not demonstrated adoption.

executive_assessment.text: Dashoguz irrigation dependence, heat and water-allocation pressures differ from Ashgabat's canal/reservoir and urban supply constraints.

Vulnerable-group participation and water-quality sensitivity require attention; women-led households and migrant families were among selected local training participants, not a representative population sample.
Independent evaluation records technical capacity gains and some water-saving finance, but also limited scaling and incomplete integration of local adaptation plans.
